extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP lawyers, in-house counsel and patent practitioners working before the Unified Patent Court (UPC)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing inventive step (obviousness) of European patents in UPC proceedings, following the UPC Court of Appeal's holistic framework and related evidential/practical considerations under Article 56 EPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the objective problem / inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the inventive concept (or the technical teaching) underlying the invention by comparing the claim as a whole in the context of the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This initial step establishes what the patented invention contributes to the state of the art. It is done from the perspective of the skilled person with common general knowledge at the priority date. To avoid hindsight, the objective problem should not contain pointers towards the claimed solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find realistic starting points in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Select prior-art starting points whose teaching would be of interest to the skilled person wishing to solve the objective problem at the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A starting point is realistic if it discloses features similar to those relevant to the claimed invention and/or addresses the same underlying problem. The relevant field includes any field in which the same or a similar problem arises and of which the skilled person is expected to be aware. There can be more than one starting point, and the invention must be inventive from each of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointer/motivation requirement from prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The skilled person needs a pointer or motivation from a realistic starting point that directs them to implement a next step toward the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claimed solution is obvious when the skilled person would take the next step either (i) prompted by the pointer or (ii) as a matter of routine, and arrive at the claimed invention. Conditional language, identification of areas for exploration, and calls for further studies cannot count as directional signposts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Would, not could — avoid hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: The assessment asks whether the skilled person would (not merely could) have arrived at the claimed invention with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is insufficient to show mere feasibility, existence of techniques to implement a change, a general interest in a target, or a broad research activity. The skilled person must be directed by the prior art and be able to predict success with some confidence appropriate to the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of success / predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: The party asserting obviousness must prove the skilled person would have expected to find the envisaged solution to the objective problem — i.e., results were clearly predictable or there was a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictability requires a rational prediction based on a scientific appraisal of known facts before the start of the research project, that the step would solve the objective problem within acceptable time limits. The strength of a pointer and field-specific scientific/physiological predictability are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstantial factors affecting reasonable expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether there is a reasonable expectation of success depends on case circumstances (technical field, practical difficulties, costs, contemporaneous work, pointer strength).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i) In unexplored technical fields it is more difficult to predict success, so expectation is lower. ii) Practical/technical difficulties and costs may deter the skilled person — if the patentee substantiates such uncertainties, the obviousness challenger must prove these would not prevent a reasonable expectation. iii) A stronger pointer lowers the threshold for expectation. iv) Contemporaneous work by others does not necessarily imply a reasonable expectation of success; it may instead indicate mere hope to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: No substitution between pointer and predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Pointer/motivation and predictability/reasonable expectation are interdependent but one cannot substitute for the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stronger pointer can increase expectation of success, but it cannot fix a predictability gap; if key scientific or physiological uncertainties persist at the priority date, there can be no reasonable expectation of success even with strong pointer(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art that teaches away or persistent uncertainties can defeat obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior-art design philosophy teaching away from the invention or unresolved physiological/technical uncertainties may defeat motivation and predictability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-priority context (later publications continuing to describe contributions as uncertain) can reinforce uncertainty. Such factors undermine both the pointer and the reasonable expectation required for obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical-use claims require meaningful therapeutic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims in 'medical use' format, the expectation required is of an effective treatment that has a meaningful therapeutic effect, not merely some degree of biological effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments must consider whether the skilled person could reasonably predict a meaningful therapeutic outcome at the priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obvious alternative suffices; improvement over prior art not necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to show improvement of the technical teaching as defined in the patent claims over the prior art; a non-obvious alternative to known solutions may be sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UPC accepts that providing a non-obvious alternative can establish inventive step even without demonstrable improvement in the claimed patent over prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee reliance on a technical effect in the application
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may rely upon a technical effect if the skilled person with common general knowledge, based on the application, would consider that technical effect as being encompassed by the technical teaching and embodied by the same originally disclosed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The technical effect must be cogently disclosed such that the skilled person at the priority date would see it as part of the invention's teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden for establishing obviousness rests with the party seeking to revoke the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That party must prove that the skilled person would have taken the next steps from prior art with a reasonable expectation of success; patentees can defend inventiveness by substantiating unattractive, uncertain, costly, or practically difficult next steps at the priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and capabilities of the skilled person
rubrics_metrics.description: The skilled person is unimaginative, has no inventive skills or imagination, and acts on pointers/motivation or routine practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the skilled person lacks inventiveness, the analysis focuses on whether prior art would have prompted a routine or motivated next step rather than on hypothetical creativity.
